verses.1: Al-Mizan holds that sūrahs opened by combinations of disjoint letters (ḥūrūf-muqaṭṭaʿah) are thematically connected with those letters, and that sūrahs sharing letters have shared themes. The connection between this sūrah and Sūrah Ṣād, particularly their accounts of the Prophets, supports this. It promises a later comprehensive discussion and comparison, including with Sūrah Yā Sīn through yāʾ and Sūrah al-Shūrā through ʿayn.
verses.2: Al-Mizan takes “mention” (dhikr) as the predicate of an implied subject: this is an account of the previously mentioned mercy of the Lord to Zachariah. That mercy is God’s answering of Zachariah’s prayer, as the ensuing narrative—“When he called upon his Lord in a low voice”—shows.
verses.3: Al-Mizan connects “when” (idh) with the Lord’s mercy. Nidāʾ and munādāt denote calling aloud, but a call may be loud while remaining private and unheard by others; this accords with Zachariah’s later coming out to his people from his place of worship. Some exegetes instead say nidāʾ conveys his sense of distance from God because of sin and adverse circumstances, like one fearing divine punishment.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan explains that Zachariah’s words introduce his request for an heir. His opening rabbī appeals for divine mercy, and the emphatic wording affirms his utter need of God. Weakness is ascribed to the bones because they support the body, while the reference to bones in general first evokes their inherent weakness before applying it to him. “My head flares with gray” vividly likens the spreading white hair to a fire spreading its blaze.

“I have never been unsuccessful in my supplication to You” most likely means that he has never been deprived or disappointed when praying: God has habitually answered his calls and petitions. Although some interpret it instead as saying that Zachariah was never wretched or disobedient toward God’s call to worship, Al-Mizan prefers the first sense. The repeated and carefully placed rabbī heightens the supplication’s eloquence, as it does later in “and make him, my Lord, one in whom You are well pleased.”
verses.5:
Al-Mizan explains mawālī primarily as Zachariah’s paternal uncles and their sons, though it has also been taken as other indirect heirs, male heirs generally, cousins alone, or heirs in general. In every case it denotes heirs other than one’s biological children. Zachariah therefore fears what these relatives will do after his death, and his words express his fear of dying without offspring to carry on from his own loins. His wife’s being ʿāqir means both that she was barren and that she had passed childbearing age. Together with his earlier old age and his record of answered prayers, these words form the prelude to his request.

“Grant me from Yourself” expresses that ordinary means had failed: Zachariah was aged and weak, and his aged wife had formerly been barren. A waliyy is one who takes charge of a person’s affairs; for a deceased person, it is one who takes charge of affairs and inherits the estate. “From the children of Jacob” may refer to Jacob son of Isaac, or, on another reported identification, to Zachariah’s wife’s relation to Jacob’s family. “Make him … pleasing” means make him marḍiyy, one with whom God is pleased in belief and action; its unrestricted wording includes beneficial knowledge and good deeds.

The commentary reads this request through Zachariah’s prayer in Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān: … My Lord! grant me from You good offspring; surely You are the Hearer of supplication (3:35-38). Seeing Mary’s sincere worship and her rank with God prompted him to seek offspring similarly favored by God. Thus “good offspring” corresponds to the heir who is made raḍiyyan, and “grant me from Yourself an heir” corresponds to his request for offspring. His concern about the mawālī further reflects their inadequacy to carry on after him.

Al-Mizan consequently rejects the view that he merely sought an unspecified successor from among his people. Hab lī, “grant me,” is fitting for a familial possession, unlike jaʿl, “make,” for a non-familial guardian or helper. Waliyy here means offspring, specifically a son, and yarithunī, “who should inherit from me,” naturally evokes inheritance of wealth and property. This material inheritance is the contextual qualifier which fixes the otherwise general waliyy as a biological heir; it is not the object of Zachariah’s worldly attachment.

The commentary rejects inheritance of Prophethood: Mary’s worship and honor did not provide a reason to seek a prophetic heir, Prophethood is not plainly hereditary, and asking that a prophet be made raḍiyyan would improperly emphasize a higher rank through a lower one. It likewise rejects making raḍiyy mean pleasing to people, since that narrows an expression encompassing every aspect of divine pleasure. Inheritance of knowledge is also unsupported, for it has no causal connection with what Zachariah witnessed in Mary; raḍiyy already includes both useful knowledge and good deeds, so knowledge need not be inserted into inheritance. Nor can inheritance mean Zachariah’s piety, closeness to God, or spiritual rank: the context calls for a son to receive what would otherwise go to his mawālī, while Prophets do not begrudge others nearness to God.

Some say he feared wicked Israelites becoming his successors in his community. Al-Mizan answers that esoteric divine succession is not hereditary, never misses its rightful recipient, and therefore gives no cause for such fear. If the succession is outward, worldly rule, it is a worldly possession analogous to property; moreover, John did not govern, and the Children of Israel had no dominion in Zachariah’s and John’s time, being under Roman rule.

Others object that a prophet as detached as Zachariah could not have worried about property, could have given it away before death, and therefore sought a son only to preserve law, Sharīʿah, or Prophethood. Al-Mizan responds that this confuses the point: he principally sought a son, as shown by … My Lord! grant me from You good offspring (3:38) and … O my Lord leave me not alone (21:89). The mention of inheritance does not make wealth his goal; it identifies the requested waliyy as a son. Without this financial-inheritance qualifier, inheritance of knowledge, Prophethood, worship, or spiritual status would not establish that a son was intended, since such inheritances do not depend on lineage.

Wanting a son is an innate human disposition, shared by Prophets and others, which divine law praises rather than repeals. A child’s continuing after a parent and receiving what the parent possessed naturally appears as a continuation of the parent’s own life and livelihood. Thus the request neither indicates attachment to worldly adornment nor makes the estate its real purpose.

Some oral traditions say that Zachariah saw out-of-season fruit with Mary and inferred that God could likewise give him a child despite old age and barrenness; on that view, however, he is said to have sought inheritance only of Prophethood, knowledge, worship, or rank. Al-Mizan finds no evidence that the sustenance in (3:37) specifically meant such fruit or that it was the motive for his request. Rather, the context, especially Mary’s gracious acceptance and growth, shows that her exceptional rank with God and provision beyond natural means prompted him to seek good offspring. He first desired a son, then, as a noble Prophet, sought a good son whom God would find pleasing.

Accordingly, “an heir who should inherit from me” means a son, described through guardianship in inheritance (wilāyah al-ʾirth), the guardianship that belongs to a child inheriting what a deceased parent leaves. Inheritance of Prophethood, knowledge, or esoteric spiritual rank, even if it may be called inheritance, is independent of lineage and lacks any convincing contextual indication here. To prefer those meanings is to abandon the immediate meaning without evidence.

verses.7:
Al-Mizan understands the verse elliptically: God answered Zachariah and called to him with the good news of John. Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ says that God responded to Zachariah and gave him John (21:90), while Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān shows that the divine message was conveyed through Angels (3:39).

God Himself named John (Yaḥyā). “We have not made before anyone his equal” may mean that no one before bore his name, and may also mean that none was his equal. His unique distinctions include receiving wisdom in childhood, being honorable and chaste, and receiving peace at birth, death, and resurrection. Though his maternal cousin, the Messiah, shared some of these epithets, he was born after John.
verses.8: Al-Mizan notes that ghulām denotes a male child or youth, and that reaching al-ʿatiyy, extreme old age, alludes to the loss of sexual capacity and the means of procreation. Zachariah’s question, despite having already mentioned his and his wife’s condition, expresses astonishment and seeks clarification about the manner of the promised birth; it is neither doubt nor denial. Unexpected good news amid apparent impediments can unsettle a person and lead him to ask for particulars, while he remains certain that it is true, as with Abraham’s request that his heart be at ease (2:260).
verses.9:
Al-Mizan takes the speaker to be God. Kadhālik, “so shall it be,” is direct speech and means that the promised matter will certainly occur as announced. The further divine speech—“It is easy for Me, and indeed I created you before, when you were nothing”—explains this assurance: God’s will does not fail, and creating a son for an aged man and barren woman is easy for Him. The creation of Zachariah from nothing dispels the occasion for amazement.

This accords with the parallel wording, “even thus God does what He pleases” (3:40): “It is easy for Me” corresponds to God’s doing whatever He pleases. Al-Mizan finds unsupported by the context the alternatives that kadhālik is attached to the second “said,” or that “your Lord says” addresses the Prophet rather than Zachariah.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan explains that, having received the glad tidings through the Angels, Zachariah requested a distinguishing sign to confirm that the call was angelic revelation rather than a satanic suggestion. He was therefore given a sign beyond Satan’s control, notwithstanding the divine immunity already granted to Prophets.

The sign was that, while fully sound in health, he would be unable to speak to people for three nights, meaning three nights and their days. His tongue was restrained from everything except remembrance of God; he could communicate with people only through signs and gestures. This is confirmed by: Your sign is that you should not speak to men for three days except by signs; and remember your Lord much and glorify Him in the evening and the morning (3:41).
verses.11: Al-Mizan, citing Majmaʿ al-bayān, explains al-miḥrāb as a place named for the worshipper’s struggle against the Devil in prayer; its root is also connected with the council of nobles where people defend their families’ interests. Fa awḥā ilayhim means that Zachariah conveyed a meaningful instruction secretly and swiftly: he signaled to his people to glorify God morning and evening.
verses.12:
Al-Mizan explains taking hold of the Book with strength as mastering its knowledge and sciences and diligently acting by its laws. John was commanded to do this in both knowledge and deed. The Book is most reasonably the Torah, or the Torah together with the earlier Prophets’ Books, since it was the Book containing the Sharīʿah of that time; it is also not far-fetched that John had a celestial book of his own.

Ḥukm does not mean Prophethood, since the Qur’an distinguishes the Book, ḥukm, and Prophethood. Nor is there evidence for reducing it to intellect, etiquette of service, or true discernment. Since ḥikma is a kind of ḥukm, Al-Mizan defines ḥukm as knowledge of true divine maʿārif and disclosure of what ordinary perception does not reveal. John was given this knowledge while still a child, before puberty.

“And tenderness from Us” means that God granted him ḥanān, compassion or sympathy. Interpretations include mercy in the sense of Prophethood or guardianship, human love for him, his own gentleness toward people, and God’s love for him. Al-Mizan takes its indefiniteness and the phrase “from Us,” used for what transcends ordinary causes, to indicate a unique divine love and affinity between God and John; this refutes the interpretations of people’s love for him or his own tenderness toward them. The following zakāt means sound, uncorrupt growth, either through God’s love and special care for John or through John’s love and affinity for his Lord, with the growth being that of the soul. It is therefore weak to take zakāt as blessing, charity, or sinlessness.

John was taqiyy, guarding against what God forbids and thereby against punishment; he was dutiful to his parents; and he was neither jabbār nor ʿaṣiyy. Jabbār denotes arrogant self-exaltation, demanding that others endure one’s will while refusing to endure anything from them, and ʿaṣiyy denotes defiance. These descriptions respectively portray his relation to his Lord, his parents, and other people. Toward people he was kind, humble, compassionate, sincere in counsel, a helper of the weak, and a guide to seekers of guidance. Thus ʿaṣiyy does not mean disobedient to his Lord.

verses.15:
Al-Mizan distinguishes salām from ʾamn: ʾamn is freedom from what one fears or hates, whereas salām means a condition in which all that one encounters suits one, without dislike or fear. The indefinite salāmun signifies magnificent peace for John on the three days that begin the worlds through which humanity passes: at birth, so that nothing impairs his happiness; at death, in a blissful barzakh; and at resurrection, in a true life free from weariness and exhaustion.

It is claimed that the qualifier ḥayyan, “alive,” implies that John will be martyred, in light of the description of martyrs as alive and provided for by their Lord (3:169). The differing tenses—“was born,” “dies,” and “is raised”—indicate that this greeting of peace accompanies him across his eternal lifetime.
verses.16: Al-Mizan explains that “the Book” may mean either the Qur’an or a sūrah, since a sūrah is part of the Book and thus scripture; there is little benefit in preferring one sense over the other. Intibādh means withdrawing from people into seclusion. The command therefore recalls to Muḥammad Mary’s account: when Mary, Amram’s daughter and the Messiah’s mother, withdrew from her family to an eastern place, apparently east of the mosque.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan explains that Mary screened herself from her family, apparently withdrawing for worship, as indicated by her sanctuary in the earlier account. The detailed report that she alternated worship between the mosque and Zachariah’s house and was visited while bathing has no support in this verse’s wording.

The subject of “there appeared” is the Spirit sent to Mary: he appeared to her as a well-made man, while remaining in himself a Spirit rather than becoming human. Since he was neither human nor jinn, he was an Angel; Qur’anic descriptions of the Angel of revelation as Gabriel, the holy or faithful Spirit, and an honored Messenger support identifying this Spirit as Gabriel. The dialogue of the “Angels” with Mary in the account in Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān is the same dialogue reported here. A plural can be used for what one speaker says because he belongs to a group sharing a form, custom, or habit. Calling him God’s Spirit confers honor and greatness. The claims that the Spirit is Jesus while Gabriel is the one who appeared, or that Rūḥannā names an angel other than Gabriel, are plainly untenable.

Tamaththul means that something appears to another in a particular form without becoming that thing. Gabriel was human in Mary’s sensory perception, but was in another form beyond her senses; he did not cease to be an Angel or essentially transform into a man. Essential transformation would be a different matter altogether. This is analogous to angels appearing as men to Abraham and Lot, and to reported manifestations of Satan, the world, a person’s deeds, or things in dreams. Such representations need not involve a thing’s changing from one inherent shape into another; indeed, many represented things have no inherent bodily shape.

Objections that Gabriel’s enormous body could not be reduced to human dimensions, that manifestation undermines certainty of identity and mutawātir reports, or that it entails appearing as every kind of animal, rest on misunderstanding tamaththul as essential transformation or on faulty assumptions about perception. The proposed answer that Gabriel merely retains some bodily parts likewise concedes the mistaken premise. Sensory perception is certainly real as perception, but what is perceived is an image within the scope of the senses, not external reality itself; whether the image corresponds to that reality is judged through thought and theoretical knowledge. The familiar errors of perception show this distinction, yet they do not invalidate ordinary reliance on sense and experience. External things, or internal states such as fear, can cause sensory images; in most cases people correctly judge the external reality, though they may err, as with a mirage.

Thus the possibility of manifestation does not destroy knowledge of identity or transmitted reports. The third objection also confuses necessary possibility with a merely conceivable mental possibility: an angel’s appearing human does not entail that it can appear as every animal, and no reliable oral evidence establishes such a restriction or extension. The same answer resolves the objection concerning mutawātir reports, since oral transmission too depends on sensory hearing.

Tamaththul is consequently an appearance in a form familiar to the perceiver and suited to its purpose: Gabriel appeared as a well-made man because messages among people are conveyed through speech and conversation. This is not sophistry. Sophistry would be a sensory image with no reality behind it at all, whereas manifestation has a reality that appears in a form the perceiver’s senses can receive. To demand more through acquired knowledge (ʿilm ḥuṣūlī) is to demand the unattainable.
verses.18: Al-Mizan explains that Mary, shocked because she took the visitor for a human intruder intending harm, immediately sought refuge in the Beneficent, whose all-encompassing mercy is sought by those devoted solely to God. Her words “if you are one guarding against evil” most aptly appeal to, and hold him to, the piety he claims or possesses: his piety ought to prevent him from harming her. Although in could be read negatively—“you are not pious, since you have invaded my privacy”—the conditional appeal better fits the context. The claim that Taqiy was a person’s name deserves no weight.
verses.19: Al-Mizan explains that Gabriel briefly identifies himself as Mary’s Lord’s messenger so that she knows he is not a human being and her fear subsides before receiving the glad tidings. Zakiyy denotes a boy who develops and grows properly. The sūrah’s stories are harmoniously arranged around God’s grants: John to Zachariah, Jesus to Mary, Isaac and Jacob to Abraham, and Aaron to Moses.
verses.20: Al-Mizan explains that Mary’s question is rhetorical: how could she have a child when no man had associated with her either lawfully in marriage or unlawfully through fornication? “Touching” can by itself cover both possibilities, while its contrast here with unchastity specifies marriage as its immediate allusion. She understood Gabriel’s promise to mean that the child would be given to her at once, and therefore denied both any prior marriage and fornication.
verses.21: Al-Mizan explains that Gabriel’s “Even so” means, “as I have described to you”: God says the miraculous birth is easy for Him. Jesus’ fatherless creation serves purposes only partly expressed: he is a sign to people through his very nature, and a mercy from God through his message and the miracles at his hands. The conjunction joins this stated purpose to further implied purposes, alluding to divine purposes too great for human comprehension or full expression. The matter has been decreed, so the birth of this rightly growing boy is inevitable and cannot be prevented by resistance or prayer.
verses.22: Al-Mizan explains that qaṣiyy means remote: after conceiving Jesus, Mary went apart with him to a place far from her family.
verses.23: Al-Mizan explains that the pains of childbirth compelled Mary, after her withdrawal from her people, to go to the trunk of a palm tree to give birth. Mention of the trunk rather than merely a palm tree suggests that it was dry and without verdure. Her wish to have died and become an insignificant forgotten thing arose from embarrassment and fear of what her people would say when they found her in this condition.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan holds that the one who called to Mary from beneath her was the newborn Jesus, not Gabriel. “From beneath her” suits a child at birth, and the surrounding pronouns refer to Jesus; the suggestion that Gabriel stood beneath a hillock has no textual support. The call followed her cry of anguish and comforted her against the especially bitter prospect, for a devout virgin from a virtuous household, of an undefendable accusation of dishonor. Jesus would defend her with decisive proof, which is why she was directed not to speak.

Sariyy more fittingly means a stream than a noble person, since the following command is to eat and drink. The entire speech encourages Mary and relieves her grief.
verses.25: Al-Mizan explains that hazz means to shake violently, and that the palm tree is the subject of its dropping fresh dates. The wording—shaking its trunk while the whole palm is said to drop fruit—suggests that the tree had been dry and then immediately put forth leaves and fresh ripe dates. Janī denotes what has been freshly picked.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan explains that “refresh the eye” means delight and happiness: Mary is to eat the fresh dates, drink from the stream, and cease grieving. Since sorrow prevents one from enjoying food and drink, the command signals consolation; regarding the accusations and questions she fears, she is to remain silent because Jesus will answer and remove them.

The commanded fast is a vow of silence, as shown by “so I shall not speak to any man today.” It was apparently a recognized practice and excuse for silence in that time. If Mary encountered someone who questioned her about the child, she was to convey by gesture that she had vowed this fast; such signification can be called “saying.” The context also permits the inference that she was instructed to undertake the vow then, so that her statement would be true. She was thus to refer the matter to Jesus rather than answer anyone herself.
verses.27: Al-Mizan explains that both pronouns refer to Jesus: Mary came to her people carrying him. Their rhetorical accusation arose from the shocking appearance of her situation despite her ascetic withdrawal, her descent from Amram, and her belonging to Aaron’s saintly family. Fariyy most aptly denotes an unprecedented, grave offense; a secondary derivation from “lie” is less supported by the following verse.
verses.28: Al-Mizan reports that Majmaʿ al-bayān gives four views of the Aaron addressed in “O sister of Aaron”: he may have been a righteous Israelite, so that “sister” means one like him; Mary’s paternal half-brother; Aaron, Moses’ brother, so that “sister” means a tribal or familial relation; or a man notorious for prostitution and immorality. Baghy means a prostitute.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan explains that Mary pointed to Jesus so that he would answer and disclose the truth, fulfilling his instruction that she not speak. Mahd has its literal sense of a baby’s cot; there is no evidence that Jesus could not already have been placed in one when the people confronted her, so proposed senses such as her lap, a rocking cradle, or merely the place where he lay are unnecessary.

The use of kāna (“was”) has been challenged because their refusal to speak concerns Jesus’ present infancy, not a past infancy. Al-Zamakhsharī’s explanation that the past tense can refer to the immediately preceding time removes the grammatical objection, but does not reach the reason for their refusal; in this reading kāna is supplementary. His other explanation, that they mean they had never spoken with those characterized by being in the cradle, is counterintuitive. The view that kāna is an emphatic supplement without tense lacks evidence and introduces needless complication. Reading man as conditional and the past tense as future is contrived.

The better possibilities are that kāna carries no temporal force within the conditional-consequent structure, or that it indicates an enduring relation between the description and its subject. Thus they mean: how can we speak to one in the earliest stage of infancy in his cradle, who will remain an infant for some time? God knows best.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan explains that Jesus’ speech from the cradle, itself miraculous, together with its truth, made clear the reality of his birth without his expressly answering the accusations against Mary. His closing greeting of peace also attests to his purity, including the legitimacy of his birth.

By first declaring himself God’s servant and later declaring God his Lord and the people’s Lord, Jesus refutes those who elevate him beyond his station. “He has given me the Book” apparently refers to the Gospel, and “made me a Prophet” states that he already possessed the Book and Prophethood, rather than merely foretelling them. At that point he was a Prophet; God later chose him as a Messenger.
verses.31: Al-Mizan explains that Jesus being mubārak wherever he is means that he is a locus of baraka, an increase of goodness: he benefits people through beneficial teaching, exhortation, moral cultivation, healing, reforming the strong, and helping the weak. Prayer and zakat were enjoined as elements of his religious law. In Qur’anic usage zakat, regularly paired with prayer, means monetary charitable expenditure, not merely purification of the soul.
verses.32: Al-Mizan explains that Jesus’ dutifulness to his mother forms part of his affection and compassion toward people, while his not being insolent and unblessed means that he is neither haughty nor wretched toward them. Jabbār describes one who makes others endure his demands while enduring nothing from them. A report from Ibn ʿAṭāʾ defines it as one who offers no sincere advice, and shaqiyy as one who does not accept sincere advice.
verses.33: Al-Mizan explains that Jesus invokes peace upon himself at the three universal stages of existence: birth, death, and resurrection. Unlike John’s greeting, which God sends and which uses the indefinite indicating a kind of peace, Jesus himself gives this greeting and uses the definite article of kind, making the expression broader and more emphatic.
verses.34: Al-Mizan holds that this verse and the next are God’s expostulatory words, while 19:36 completes Jesus’ speech. “Such is Jesus, son of Mary” refers to the whole preceding account: his birth, servitude to God, receipt of the Book, and Prophethood. Qawl al-ḥaqq means, through an implied “I say,” the true statement concerning Jesus, about whom people dispute. Though some take it as a laudatory title, “the Word of Truth,” for Jesus, the first meaning is supported by the parallel expression “the truth from your Lord.”
verses.35: Al-Mizan explains that the verse rejects the Christian claim that the Messiah is God’s son. God’s decree—when He says “Be,” and it is—proves the claim impossible. A son is ordinarily wanted for assistance, but God needs no assistance and never fails to accomplish what He wills. Moreover, sonship entails a part separated from the father and gradually raised until it becomes like him; God needs neither such gradualness in His acts nor any likeness to Himself. What He wills exists without delay or transition.
verses.36: Al-Mizan holds that this is part of Jesus’ speech, joined to “Surely I am a servant of God.” Its occurrence as Jesus’ direct address in the accounts in Sūrah Āl-ʿImrān and Sūrah al-Zukhruf confirms this, while neither the context nor the wording supports treating it as a new statement by God or an instruction to the Prophet. Jesus closes by acknowledging that he has a Lord, just as he began by declaring his servitude, thereby completing the refutation of those who raise him above his station.
verses.37: Al-Mizan explains that aḥzāb are separate groups, each holding an opinion different from the others. “From among them” indicates that some among those concerned remained firm upon the truth, rather than being a superfluous addition. Wayl is a threat of severe punishment, and mashhad denotes the place or occasion of witnessing. The verse therefore threatens the disbelieving groups over their disagreement concerning Jesus.
verses.38: Al-Mizan explains that on the Day of Resurrection those who disputed the truth will hear and see it with complete clarity. Yet the clause concerning the unjust prevents the inference that this disclosure will guide or benefit them: Judgment Day is requital, not a time for fresh action and future reward. They encounter only what they did and acquired beforehand. Their disposition for error became entrenched in this world, and death ends their freedom to remediate it; they remain compelled within the error they made for themselves. Therefore the manifestation of reality does not avail them. The interpretation that the Prophet is merely commanded to make people hear and see by warning them is wholly inapplicable.
verses.39: Al-Mizan explains that “when the matter shall have been decided” defines the Day of Intense Regret. Regret becomes immeasurable when one irrevocably loses the object of one’s deepest desire and happiness, something one could have attained and would endure hardship to preserve. The people’s negligence and unbelief in this world divert them from the path to eternal happiness: belief in God alone and denial that He has a son or partner. When the matter is decreed, they will be cut off from that happiness and face inevitable eternal doom, producing the intense regret against which they are warned.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse confirms and clarifies the preceding decree of the matter: God’s decision is easy because, when people die, they leave the earth and all their possessions behind for God, and return to Him. More precisely, God alone remains when the earth and humanity come to an end; He takes possession of the earth’s very existence and traces, and of all that people had owned. Their return means that all are gathered before Him, explaining the divine inheritance without reducing the verse to repetition.

The verse fittingly concludes Jesus’ story because God’s inheritance of everything is proof that He has no need for a son: a father seeks a son as an heir, whereas the One who inherits all things needs none.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan takes ṣiddīq as an intensive noun meaning one exceptionally truthful, whose words and deeds never conflict. Abraham displayed this truthfulness by professing tawḥīd alone in an idolatrous world, arguing with his father and people, resisting the king of Babel, breaking the idols, enduring the fire, and finally withdrawing from them as he had promised; God then granted him Isaac, Jacob, and the other stated gifts. The alternative derivation from taṣdīq, making it one who repeatedly confirms truth in word and deed, is substantially similar but unlikely, since such intensive forms are rarely derived from verbal forms other than the first form ṣadaqa. An editor notes that the person addressed as “O my father” was later identified by the author as Abraham’s uncle, maternal grandfather, or stepfather rather than his biological father.

The commentary derives nabī, “Prophet,” from nabaʾ, “a tiding”: a Prophet receives tidings of the unseen through divine revelation. It reports, alternatively, a derivation from al-nubuwwa, sublimity, referring to the loftiness of his rank.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan holds that “When he said to his father” is a temporal adverbial clause attached to Abraham, and that connecting it instead to “a truthful man” or “a Prophet” is an artificial reading. Its introduction of Abraham and his Prophethood corresponds to the introduction of Mary in the Book.

Abraham first exposes idol worship as futile and false, then declares that he possesses knowledge his father lacks and calls him to follow the path of truth, lest he come under Satan’s guardianship. Calling idols “what neither hears nor sees” both rebukes their worship and contains the proof of their impotence. Worship requires an object aware of the worshiper’s submission; inanimate idols neither hear nor see. Moreover, people worship and pray in hope of benefit or protection from harm, but idols can provide neither, so their worship has no effect.

The commentary reports from its exegesis of Sūrah al-Anʿām [The Cattle] that Abraham’s addressee was his uncle, maternal grandfather, or stepfather, not his father. Grammarians hold that the final tāʾ in yā abatī and yā ummatī replaces the first-person possessive yā only in the vocative; it cannot be used outside it, as in “my father said.”
verses.43:
Al-Mizan explains that, after showing idol worship to be invalid, Abraham tells his father that he has knowledge the latter lacks and should therefore follow him. A ṣirāṭan sawiyyan is a path so plain that its traveler cannot go astray. Its indefinite form indicates not a previously known path but a straight path of which his father is ignorant: since he must travel some path, he should leave the crooked one and follow Abraham to a straight one.

The words “truly the knowledge has come to me” show that Abraham had received knowledge of the truth before his prophetic call and this debate. They confirm that he had already been given knowledge of God and experientially beholding (mushāhada) the dominion (malakūt) of the Heavens and earth before arguing with his father and people. His promised guidance means showing the way, not bringing a person to the destination; the latter belongs to an Imām, and Abraham had not yet been made one. This accords with: … He said: Surely I will make you an Imam of men (2:124).
verses.44:
Al-Mizan explains that “serve not Satan” does not specifically prohibit worship of idols representing jinn, though idolaters also worshiped images of jinn, Angels, and holy people. Here ʿibāda means obedience: Abraham forbids obedience to Satan, whose commands include appointing objects of worship besides God. Calling this obedience Satan’s worship also marks it as intrinsically evil.

Idol worship is not merely futile; it exposes its practitioner to ruin and Satan’s guardianship. Since God alone deserves worship and is the source of all beneficence (raḥmah), idol worship results from Satan’s enticement and disobedience to Him. Satan commands nothing pleasing to the Beneficent, but only what deprives a person of His beneficence, especially by violating the exclusive duty of worshiping Him alone. The disobedient person risks being cut off from the guidance that leads to felicity: God ceases to be his guardian, while Satan becomes his master and guardian (mawlā), and he Satan’s bound subordinate (waliyy).

The use of al-Raḥmān rather than Allah in both verses is consequential. Because He is the source of all beneficence and blessing, persisting in disobedience to Him is especially vile, and His beneficence being withheld gives cause to fear punishment, divine retribution (naqmah), and wretchedness (shaqwah). Thus the punishment Abraham fears is not, as some exegetes claim, punishment in the Hereafter, but abandonment (khidhlān): the withholding of beneficence that leaves one to oneself and under Satan’s custody.
