verses.46: Al-Mizan, citing Majmaʿ al-bayān, explains that raghiba ʿan means to dislike, the opposite of raghiba fī, to desire; intihāʾ is desisting after a prohibition; rajm is stoning, usually to death; hajr is separation; and maliyyan means a long time. Azar therefore threatens Abraham with death by stoning—the humiliating execution of one cast out—and expels him.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan explains ḥafiyy as one who is dutiful and kind, attending successively and graciously even to another’s smallest needs. In answer to his father’s threatening ignorance, Abraham invokes peace—beneficence and assurance—promises to seek forgiveness for him, and promises to withdraw from him, his people, and their objects of worship. This is the conduct of the noble-minded toward the ignorant. Some exegetes take “peace” as a farewell demanded by “leave me,” but the commentary notes that Abraham’s withdrawal from his father and people occurred only after a not-short interval.

Abraham’s prayer for his polytheist father means that he had not yet known him to be Satan’s friend in the sense of one whose polytheism was ingrained, who stubbornly opposed truth, and who was God’s enemy. His earlier “surely I fear” instead allows that the man was ignorant and weak and might follow truth once it was made clear. Divine mercy may extend to such a person. Abraham’s promise sought to soften his father’s heart; it expressed hope, not certainty, of forgiveness, as indicated by “surely He is ever affectionate to me.” His later disavowal, once his father’s enmity to God became clear, confirms that he had previously hoped he was not an enemy of God despite his polytheism. This hope can concern the ignorant, not one set on opposing truth (muʿānid).

The commentary rejects the claim that he prayed simply because such prayer was then legally permissible and was prohibited only later, judging it incompatible with the Qur’anic account. It likewise rejects the suggestions that the prayer was conditional on repentance or meant only protection from worldly punishment, the latter being an unsupported restriction. The strongest alternative—that asking forgiveness metonymically means asking for repentance and faith, its prerequisites—is still far-fetched. The words are an appeal meant to make his father receptive, for which asking forgiveness is more fitting than explicitly asking for his guidance and success in repentance. Abraham’s prayer resembles his general supplication for polytheists who disobeyed him.
verses.48: Al-Mizan reads Abraham’s words as a promise to separate himself from his people and their idols, to be alone with his Lord, and to pray sincerely in hope that he will not remain unblessed in calling upon Him. He is hopeful rather than certain because prayer and devotion do not impose anything upon God; reward and felicity are favors from Him alone. Since final outcomes and the unseen belong to God’s knowledge, the believer must remain between fear and hope.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan suggests that Isaac is named, rather than Abraham’s other son, because the passage concerns prophetic succession in the Israelite line: Jacob follows Isaac because many Prophets descended from him, as indicated by “each one of them We made a Prophet.”

It holds that the mercy granted to them in (19:50) may mean Imamate, supported by: And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, a son’s son, and We made (them) all good. And We made them Imams who guided (people) by Our command … (21:72-73). It may instead mean support by the Holy Spirit (rūḥ al-qudus), as suggested by: … and We revealed to them the doing of good (21:73), or general divine guardianship (muṭlaq al-wilāyah al-ʾilāhiyyah).
verses.50: Al-Mizan reports that lisān denotes either laudatory or disparaging mention among people. Joined to ṣidq, “truthfulness,” it means praise free of falsehood; ʿaliyyan means high in rank and quality. The verse thus means that God left for them beautiful, truthful, and highly distinguished praise.
verses.51: Al-Mizan explains that Moses being mukhlaṣ, “devoted,” means that God rendered him exclusively His: neither his self nor his deeds contained any share for other than God. This is the highest degree of servitude. The distinction between a Messenger and a Prophet is treated elsewhere in the commentary.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan explains that ʿayman, “the right,” describes jānib, “side,” and thus refers to the mountain’s right side. Citing Majmaʿ al-bayān, it explains najiyy, in the sense of munājī, as one with whom another speaks confidentially.

The drawing of Moses near is apparently figurative, although the gift occurred at the blessed side of the mountain where God spoke to him. It resembles a master calling a humble servant close and making him a confidant, thereby enabling him to receive what others cannot receive.
verses.53: Al-Mizan takes God’s gift of Aaron as a Prophet to Moses to allude to the answer to Moses’ first supplication at the mountain: “And give to me a helper from my family: Aaron, my brother, Strengthen my back by him, And associate him (with me) in my affair (20:29-32).”
verses.54:
Al-Mizan notes disagreement over the Ishmael intended. The majority identify him as Ishmael son of Abraham and explain his separate mention, rather than inclusion with Isaac and Jacob, by his special rank. Another view identifies him as Ishmael son of Ezekiel, an Israelite Prophet, arguing that Abraham’s son would have been mentioned alongside Isaac and Jacob.

The commentary finds the majority’s explanation weak: had Ishmael son of Abraham been singled out for his rank, he would more appropriately have been mentioned after Abraham and before Moses, rather than after Moses.
verses.55: Al-Mizan explains ahl as Ishmael’s nearest relations among his offspring, clan, and people; the alternative interpretation, his nation, lacks evidence. It also rejects the claim that God’s being well pleased with him concerns Ishmael himself but not his deeds. The wording is unrestricted, so there is no basis to exclude his deeds from what made him pleasing to his Lord.
verses.56: Al-Mizan reports that exegetes identify Idrīs with the Prophet Enoch, one of Noah’s ancestors mentioned in Genesis. He was called Idrīs because of his abundant study (dars).
verses.57:
Al-Mizan holds that the sūrah’s context may permit the inference that Idrīs’s “high place” was a degree of divine proximity, since its accounts concern the spiritual stations of Prophethood and guardianship. A merely physical ascent to the edge of the atmosphere would carry no particular distinction. A hadith-based interpretation instead says that God raised him to, and kept him in, one of the Heavens; as a miraculous display of divine power, this would itself be an honor.

On the interpretation that the Ishmael in 19:54-55 is Ishmael son of Ezekiel, those verses contain his only Qur’anic account. They praise him as truthful to his promise, one who enjoined prayer and almsgiving, one pleasing to his Lord, and a Messenger Prophet. A narration from al-Ṣādiq identifies him not as Abraham’s son but as a Prophet sent to his people, who scalped him and skinned his face. When an Angel offered to do whatever he wished, he answered that the Prophets and what had been done to them were a sufficient example and consolation for him. A version transmitted in ʿIlal al-sharāʾiʿ through Abī Baṣīr adds that he had a good example in al-Ḥusayn.

A report from Abū l-Ḥasan al-Riḍā explains that Ishmael was called truthful in his promise because he waited a year for a man to whom he had made a promise. Similar wording is reported from al-Ṣādiq, while Majmaʿ al-bayān gives it without a chain. Tafsīr, Al-Qummī likewise says that Ishmael son of Ezekiel waited a whole year for his companion. Al-Mizan explains that he had not stipulated an hour, a day, or any other limit; because the promise was unqualified, truthfulness required him to remain where he had promised until his companion returned.

The commentary relates keeping promises to the degree of knowledge and certitude, as with love, will, resolve, faith, reliance on God, and submission to Him. Faith mixed with error and sin is its lowest level, whereas it may become pure of latent association with God and detach the heart from all besides Him. Likewise, one who has promised without fixing a time may wait only an hour or two according to ordinary social loyalty; may wait until nightfall as the maximum reasonable period; or may adhere to the literal force of the unrestricted promise for however long it takes. Strong souls do not speak except within their power to fulfil their words, and, having spoken, let nothing divert them from what they resolved. A narration says that the Prophet waited three days by the Kaaba in Mecca for a Companion who had forgotten their arrangement. This is the level of the quintessentially truthful, the ṣiddīqīn, who do not say they will do something and then fail to do it.

Al-Mizan observes that Idrīs is mentioned in the Qur’an only in (19:56-57) and in “And Ishmael and Enoch [Idrīs] and Ezekiel [Dhū l-Kifl]; all were of the patient ones; And We caused them to enter into Our mercy, surely they were of the good ones (21:85-86).” These verses praise him as a truthful Prophet, one of the patient and good, and one raised to a high place.

A long hadith from al-Bāqir recounts that Idrīs was commissioned during the reign of a tyrant who killed a believing landowner on false testimony in order to seize his land. God sent Idrīs to warn the king that He would avenge the murdered believer, overthrow his kingdom, devastate his city, and punish his wife, who had advised the crime. The king expelled Idrīs and sought to kill him. Idrīs left with believing companions, and God told him to depart from the township; he then asked that rain be withheld until he was asked to pray for it.

According to this narration, after God destroyed the first king and his city, another tyrant ruled there, while drought afflicted the people for twenty years. They repented and pleaded with God, who told Idrīs that He had mercy on them but that Idrīs’s condition prevented the rain. Idrīs nevertheless refused to ask for it. God then withheld the food ordinarily brought to him by an Angel for three days and reproved him for grieving over his own hunger while not grieving over the people’s twenty years of distress. Idrīs was sent down to earn his own living.

The report continues that, while starving, he asked an old woman for one of her two loaves, which were for herself and her son. They divided the child’s portion, but the boy died in anxiety over it. Idrīs restored him to life by God’s permission, and the woman recognized him and announced his return. The townspeople begged him to pray for rain, but he required their tyrant and all the inhabitants to come barefoot and request it. When the tyrant first sent forty men to seize Idrīs, he prayed against them and they died; five hundred further men then begged for mercy and conveyed his condition. The tyrant and the people came humbly and barefoot, Idrīs prayed, and immediate, overwhelming rain fell upon them.

A hadith from al-Ṣādiq says that the mosque of al-Sahla was Idrīs’s house, where he used to sew. Many biographers and historians also say that he was the first to write with a pen and the first to sew. Tafsīr, Al-Qummī states that he was called Idrīs because of his abundant study (dars) of books.

Some oral traditions interpret the high place through a story of an Angel whose wing was cut off after God was angry with him. Idrīs prayed for the Angel, whose wing was restored; the Angel then carried Idrīs to the fourth Heaven, where the Angel of death took his soul between the fourth and fifth Heavens. Something similar is narrated from the Prophet. Al-Mizan judges both reports unusable because their chains are weak—particularly the second, which includes Mufaḍḍal b. Ṣāliḥ, described as a liar who fabricated hadith—and because their premise that an Angel sinned contradicts the Book’s plain teaching that Angels are infallible and free from sin and error.

Reports summarized from Ibn ʿAbbās and others tell of Idrīs praying that the Angel carrying the sun be relieved of its heat, becoming intimate with that Angel, and seeking an intercession with the Angel of death to delay his death for greater worship. The Angel of death instead found that Idrīs was to die where the sun rises, and the Angel returned to find him dead. Kaʿb’s version makes Idrīs’s companion the Angel who carried up his extraordinary deeds, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that he died between the Angel’s wings. Another report attributed to the Prophet says that Idrīs asked the Angel of death to let him experience death, see hell, and see Heaven; after entering Heaven, he argued that he had fulfilled the conditions of death and coming to hell and could not be expelled from Heaven. A version from Wahb says he remained alive, worshipping in the fourth Heaven and enjoying Heaven. Al-Ḥakīm’s al-Mustadrak ʿalā l-Ṣaḥīḥayn reports from Samura a physical description of Idrīs and says that God raised him to the sixth Heaven because of the earth’s wrongdoing. Al-Mizan says that a careful critic should have no doubt that these narrations are Isrāʾīliyyāt, fabrications based on Judeo-Christian tradition introduced by forgery, and that they are rejected by the principles of Islamic sciences and the religion’s agreed fundamentals.

Al-Qafaṭī’s biographical report calls Idrīs Hermes and records disagreements among philosophers about his origin, education, and teachers. One account makes him Egyptian, identifies him by Greek and Hebrew names, and says that God raised him from Egypt at eighty-two. Another makes him a native of Babel and a descendant of Seth (Shīth), from whom he learned in his early life. In the latter account, after receiving Prophethood he called the descendants of Adam away from corruption and from violating the law of Adam and Seth; when most disobeyed, he and his followers migrated toward the Nile. There he and they called people to obedience and moral reform. God taught him the people’s seventy-two languages, and he taught sciences, organized cities and their policies, derived wisdom (ḥikma) and astronomy through divinely granted knowledge of the celestial sphere and the calculation of time, and established appropriate social and political norms for regions under four kings.

The commentary says that such hadiths and reports concern prehistoric events and therefore cannot be relied on greatly. Yet the persistent remembrance, reverence, and attribution of the fundamentals of knowledge to Idrīs by philosophers and learned people across generations indicate that he was among the oldest father figures of knowledge, perhaps the first: a figure who led humanity into deductive thought and inspired its continuing search for deeper divine knowledge.
verses.58:
Al-Mizan holds that ulāʾika (“these”) refers to the figures previously named in the sūrah: Zachariah, John, Mary, Jesus, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Ishmael, and Enoch. Their stories supply the examples from which verses 58–60 are deduced. Grammatically, “these” is the subject, “on whom God bestowed favors” describes it, and “when the communications of the Beneficent were recited to them, they fell in prostration and weeping” is its predicate. Although “on whom God bestowed favors” could itself be treated as a first predicate, with the latter clause as a second, this does not accord as well with the sūrah’s purpose.

God’s unrestricted bestowal of favor means blessing unaccompanied by wretchedness, which is complete felicity (saʿādah) and success. These people are therefore upon the straight path, secure from wrath and misguidance; such security and guidance belong to those whose faith is not mixed with iniquity. Their adopted way of life is consequently itself the path to felicity.

Al-Mizan takes min in “from among the Prophets” and “and of those whom We guided and chose” as partitive. It may be explanatory only if “these” is understood as examples of the wider class of felicitous people, so that the sense includes both the named persons and their like among Prophets and the guided and chosen. “Of the seed of Adam” qualifies the Prophets and is likewise partitive, not explanatory. “Those whom We carried with Noah” is joined to the seed of Adam and means those carried in the ark and their descendants; “the seed of Abraham and Israel” is joined to “from among the Prophets.”

The verse thus divides the favored Prophets into four overlapping groups: the seed of Adam, those carried with Noah, the seed of Abraham, and the seed of Israel. Although each later group falls within the preceding ones, their separate mention apparently alludes to the repeated descent of Prophethood and felicity upon humankind at four appointed stages. Among the persons previously recounted, Enoch belongs to the seed of Adam; Abraham to those carried with Noah; Isaac and Jacob to Abraham’s seed; and Zachariah, John, Jesus, Moses, Aaron, and Ishmael to Israel’s seed.

“And of those whom We guided and chose” is joined to “from among the Prophets,” but denotes favored persons who are not Prophets: the truthful, martyrs, and pious. Divine favor is not confined to Prophets, and Mary, whose story is included here although she was not a Prophetess, is one of the truthful. Al-Mizan rejects the claim that min here is explanatory in a way that makes those guided and chosen merely Prophets possessing guidance and chosenness; this conflicts with the context and apparent meaning. A conjunction need not join two sets with no shared instances; it joins the complete descriptions on each side, which need not be identical. It also rejects attaching this clause to “the seed of Adam.”

The interpretation attributed to Abū Muslim, which begins a new sentence at “and of those whom We guided,” is rejected as an unsupported inference of an omitted subject. It also ruins the passage’s purpose: to contrast the favored servants’ submission and humility with the later people who neglected prayer and followed desires. That purpose requires the clause about prostration and weeping to be the predicate of “these.”

Sujjadan is the plural of sājid, “prostrate,” and bukiyyan the plural of bākī, “weeping.” Their falling in prostration and weeping is apparently a metonymy respectively for complete submissiveness (khudūʿ) and complete humility (khushūʿ). Accordingly, the Beneficent’s communications and their recitation most suitably mean the mention of anything pertaining to Him. Al-Mizan rejects restrictive readings that make the communications only heavenly scriptures or verses about punishment, prostration only prayer or the prostration required on hearing certain verses, and weeping merely literal weeping at recitation.

The verse therefore means, and God knows best, that the favored persons include Prophets from the stated lines and non-Prophets whom God guided and chose, and that they are overcome by humility and submission whenever His remembrance and signs are mentioned. The wording does not confine this conduct to the past or future; it classifies people across time into righteous predecessors, depraved successors, and those who repent and do good deeds.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan explains that khalf means a bad successor or substitute, in contrast to khalaf, a good one, though the two are rarely used conversely. Ḍayāʿ denotes something becoming invalid or lost through negligence, while ghayy is the opposite of rushd: an error akin to ḍalāl that leads to loss or perdition, whereas hudā is taking the road that reaches one’s goal.

The verse describes an evil generation succeeding the servants on whom God bestowed favor, whose way had been humble, devout worship. These successors squandered the inherited heritage of prayer and treated submission to God lightly, turning instead to desires that diverted them from striving toward and directing themselves to Him.

Aḍāʿū al-ṣalāt does not mean that they simply ceased praying altogether. It means that they corrupted prayer through neglect, failed to take it seriously, and eventually made alterations to it and forsook it after accepting it. They were bad heirs to the divine religion: they neglected prayer, the sole pillar of worship and servitude to God, and followed desires that turned them from the truth.

Exegetes explain “they will meet perdition” as punishment for their error. Alternatively, Al-Mizan considers it possible that neglecting prayer and following desires is a path whose very end is ghayy. They meet this perdition either, or in both ways, when realities become manifest on the Day of Resurrection, and when error settles in their hearts so that they become friends (awliyāʾ) of Satan. In either case, the expression is a subtle metonymy.
verses.60:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse excepts from the preceding threat those who repent, believe, and do good deeds. By these acts they return to God and are joined with those upon whom He bestowed favor: they are with them, though not of them.

“Those shall enter the Garden” states the effect in place of its cause. Its underlying sense is that they will receive their full reward, as shown by the assurance that they will not be dealt with unjustly. Freedom from injustice entails receiving the full reward, although it does not itself entail entering Paradise.
verses.61:
Al-Mizan explains that ʿadn means residence, so “Gardens of perpetuity” signifies the enduring residence of those who enter Paradise. The Beneficent’s promise is “while unseen” because its object is not perceptible to those promised it, and its being maʾtiyyan means that it will certainly not be broken.

Majmaʿ al-bayān says that the grammatical object is used while the subject is intended: what one reaches also reaches one, as in saying either that one reached fifty years or that fifty years came to one. Some exegetes say that the promised thing is Heaven, which believers reach.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan describes the absence of vain discourse as one of Heaven’s most distinctive attributes, repeatedly foretold in the Qur’an. Salām is excepted from laghu by a disjoint exception (ʾistithnāʾ munfaṣil), since peace is not a kind of vain discourse.

Salām, “peace,” is close in meaning to ʾamn, “safety,” but differs from it. To say that someone is in safety from one means that nothing harmful will come to him from that person; to say “peace be unto you” means that nothing he encounters from that speaker will harm him. The inhabitants of Heaven will hear peace from the Angels and from their companions.

Their sustenance “morning and evening” is a metonymy for provision received continuously and without interruption.
verses.63: Al-Mizan explains that irth and wirātha mean property, or something similar, passing to another after its former holder departs through death, evacuation, or the like. Since the divine promise makes Heaven available to every person on the condition of faith and righteous action, its inheritance by Godwary servants means that Paradise is confined to them, excluding those who neglected prayer and followed base desires. The verse thus combines the notions of inheritance and reward.
verses.64:
Al-Mizan explains tanazzul as a slow, unhurried descent performed submissively under a command. The restrictive wording, “we do not descend but by the command of your Lord,” means that the Angels descend solely by God’s command; they do not disobey Him or act independently.

The phrase “to Him belongs whatever is before us and whatever is behind us and whatever is between these” should not be confined to temporal divisions such as past, present, and future, or to spatial divisions such as heaven, earth, and the space between them. Such readings lack evidence and sometimes improperly ascribe human conditions to Angels. Rather, what is before them is their actions, what they govern, and the effects of those actions; what is behind them is the prior causes of their existence; and what is between these is their own existence. The expression therefore encompasses them wholly under God’s ownership: He owns their existence and all that pertains to it.

This ownership is real rulership, in which none has any disposal or power except by His permission and will. The Angels neither act nor will anything apart from what God commands and wills; consequently, an Angel descends only by his Lord’s command. The ownership clause thus explains their commanded descent, while “your Lord is not forgetful” completes the explanation. God does not neglect anything in His kingdom in a way that would disrupt the wise ordering of affairs, such as withholding a command to descend when it is due or issuing it when it is not.

The commentary rejects the interpretation that “your Lord is not forgetful” merely means that He has not forsaken His Prophets. Although that reading may accord in one respect with the stated reason for revelation, it makes the preceding ownership clause, and the subsequent reference to the Lord of the Heavens and the earth, incongruous.
verses.65:
Al-Mizan takes “The Lord of the Heavens and the earth and what is between them” as explaining the preceding declaration that all that is before, behind, and between the Angels belongs to God. Since a lord (rabb) owns and manages the affairs of what he rules, God’s ownership and His freedom from forgetfulness necessarily follow from His lordship over the heavens, the earth, and all between them.

The command, “so serve Him and be patient in His service,” follows from this lordship. The Angels descend only at the command of the Prophet’s Lord and convey words that are God’s words and a call that is His call; therefore He alone must be served steadfastly. There is no other lord to whom one may turn, worship exclusively, or associate with Him. The commentary rejects readings that make this command follow merely from the statement of divine lordship or from the assertion that God has not forgotten the Prophet, judging their difficulty evident.

“Do you know anyone equal (samiyy) to Him?” completes the rationale for exclusive, persevering worship. Samiyy means one who shares the same name. Since the verse establishes God’s absolute lordship, the name at issue is al-Rabb: there is no other being possessing lordship who can rightly be called Lord and thereby justify turning from God to worship another. Al-Mizan therefore rejects interpretations of samiyy as a metaphorical “like,” a literal or nonliteral son, or as referring instead to the names Allāh, al-Ilāh, al-Raḥmān, or to such descriptions as Creator, Provider, Giver and Taker of Life, and One able to reward and punish.

The repeated expression “your Lord,” rather than “our Lord,” prepares this affirmation of divine Unity: the Lord by whose command the Angels descend is the Prophet’s Lord, and the call they bring is His call. The two commands—to serve God and to remain constant in His service—are inseparable and together require worship to be exclusive to Him. The fa in “therefore serve Him” may also be understood to confirm the preceding discourse rather than make these verses a complete digression.

The commentary accordingly portrays the Angel of revelation as declaring that he neither had descended nor would descend on his own initiative, but only by his Lord’s command and with His message. God is the Lord of the Prophet and of all things, so the Prophet must serve Him alone; the verses strengthen his heart and reinforce the preceding call. This resembles a king’s messenger who says that he comes by the king’s command, delivers the king’s own words, and calls the recipient to obey the sole king. The messenger’s words can thus be his own words while also constituting the king’s commanded message. Al-Mizan judges this explanation more fitting to the verses than oral reports about their occasion of revelation, given those reports’ discrepancies and weakness.
verses.66:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse voices the unbelievers’ denial of resurrection as impossible. Though such people include polytheists and those who deny a Creator, the statement is attributed to “man” rather than expressly to unbelievers because rational perception should lead man to something better. The subsequent threat of gathering them with the Satans also permits “man” here to refer specifically to deniers of resurrection.

Their doubt is especially astonishing because they know that God created them when they were nothing; recreating them should therefore not be difficult to believe. The repetition of insān in the reply, “Does not man remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?”, stresses that a human being ought not reject the recurrence of what he has already witnessed and not forgotten. The present tense in “And says man” may further indicate that this disbelief or doubt persists among its adherents.
verses.67: Al-Mizan says the rhetorical question expresses surprise that a person could forget the first creation, which proves God’s power to resurrect the dead. The objection that a likeness is not the identical person concerns only the body: human identity lies in the distinct self, not the body. Although the recreated body resembles rather than is the original body, joining the same self to it restores the very same human being. Bodily change and replacement during aging do not destroy personal identity; likewise, the Angel of death takes the self intact from the body rather than allowing it to be lost.
verses.68:
Al-Mizan holds that the pronouns in “We will most certainly gather them together” and “cause them to be present” refer to the unbelievers, not to believers and unbelievers alike. The wrathful, punitive tone of verses 68–70 confines their subject to the disbelievers.

Jathiyy is the plural of jāthin and means kneeling. A report attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās derives it from juthwah, a mass of dust and stones, yielding the sense that those summoned in throngs will be piled together; the commentary considers this interpretation more fitting to the context. Thus the unbelievers will be gathered from their graves with the Satans who are their guardians because of their unbelief, or with their devilish peers and associates, and will be made present around Hell for punishment, kneeling in humiliation or arriving group after group.

“So by your Lord!” shifts from addressing the unbelievers to speaking of them. This may preserve the rhetorical pattern associated with the expression “your Lord.”
verses.69:
Al-Mizan explains nazʿ as drawing forth, shiʿa as a group united in an aim or belief, and ʿitiyyā as rebellious disobedience. It is likely that “of them him who is most ostentatiously rebellious against the Beneficent” is an interrogative clause functioning as the object of “We will most certainly draw forth,” emphasizing the careful determination of the most rebellious in every group. The intended people are thus the chiefs and leaders of error. Another view is that the most rebellious will be taken first, followed successively by those less rebellious until all are taken.

The shift to the third person in “against the Beneficent” underscores the gravity of rebelling against the One whose beneficence encompasses all things and from whom they receive nothing but beneficence.
verses.70: Al-Mizan explains ṣaliyy as suffering the heat of fire. God therefore certainly knows best those most deserving of Hellfire and its heat; the degrees of their punishment and the levels they merit are not obscure to Him.
verses.71:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse addresses all mankind, believers as well as unbelievers, as the following deliverance of those who fear God shows. Wāriduhā refers to Hell. The claim that the pronoun concerns only the unbelievers of the preceding verses is rejected by the context.

Wurūd originally means seeking or coming to water, the opposite of ṣudūr, going away from it. Al-Rāghib, in al-Mufradāt fī gharīb al-Qurʾān, explains that it was extended to other things: a wārid comes to water, and may also be one sent ahead to draw it. This usage underlies the view that people will come upon and look down upon Hell without entering it. The cited usage concerning those kept far from Hell does not preclude entry, however: they may be removed after entering, or God may prevent them from hearing its sound, as He protected Abraham from the fire’s heat.

Possibly the majority of exegetes take wurūd here as entry into Hell, citing verses in which people are brought to the Fire. They also appeal to the next verse’s “We will leave (nadharu) the unjust therein,” since leaving someone somewhere implies that he entered and settled there. Some say everyone enters; others restrict entry to those without fear of God by reading “of you” as “of them.” The latter view is not supported by the context of “And We will deliver those who fear (God).”

The commentary maintains that wurūd itself does not mean entry. In such expressions as “they would not have come to it (mā waradūha)” (21:99), coming upon and looking down at the Fire is more fitting; similarly, Pharaoh leads his people to the Fire but does not himself put them into it. The wrongdoers’ entry in the following verse is established by nadharu, not by wāriduhā. Conversely, delivering the Godwary need not mean that they entered: they may be saved after entry or saved at the brink after witnessing it. Oral traditions describe the event, not the lexical meaning of wāriduhā, and cannot prove that it means entry.

The suggestion that the verse means merely that all humans are naturally fit to enter Hell, since their goodness is from God and only evil remains to them, is contradicted by “this is an unavoidable decree of your Lord”: their coming is brought about by God’s unavoidable decree, not simply by human nature. The sound sense of wurūd is intentionally coming to and standing over Hell. This does not determine whether all or only the unjust subsequently enter it. The unavoidable decree concerns this coming itself, or the whole preceding declaration; ḥatm, jazm, and qaṭʿ all express its certainty and inevitability. God alone has decreed it upon Himself, for no higher judge can bind Him.
verses.72:
Al-Mizan explains that “We will leave the unjust therein” means that the unjust enter Hell and remain there kneeling. Deliverance of the Godwary does not necessarily mean that they enter it, unless both clauses are taken as occurring after entry. Calling those left behind “the unjust” indicates that their injustice is the cause of their remaining there.

Together, verses 71–72 mean that every person, Godwary and unjust alike, will come upon Hell by a decree that the Lord has imposed upon Himself. He will then deliver those who guarded against it, while leaving the unjust kneeling there because of their injustice.
verses.73:
Al-Mizan explains maqām as an abode and nadiyyan as a gathering, with some restricting the latter to a consultative assembly. The disbelievers are speaking directly to the believers; although some take the lām in lil-mu’minīn causally, as speech intended to lead them astray, the direct, communicative sense better suits the context. Likewise, “them” refers to people generally, of whom the disbelievers are an expressly named subgroup and the believers the other subgroup.

“Which of the two parties” is a rhetorical question concerning the disbelievers and believers. It asserts, under the guise of a question, that the disbelievers possess superior dwellings and company, whereas the believers are largely poor and enslaved. Calling them “the two parties” suggests that the believers themselves supposedly know and would concede this comparison. The disbelievers infer that worldly comfort is the whole of happiness; hence they regard their own path as felicitous and true.
verses.74:
Al-Mizan explains qarn as people alike or contemporaneous in an age, athāth as abundant household goods, and riʾy as the visible object or outward appearance, unlike raʾy and ruʾya, which denote the act of seeing or forming an opinion.

The disbelievers treat their superior possessions and social setting as proof that their way of life is superior and the Prophetic call false. They forget that human felicity belongs to everlasting life: the few days of this world cannot replace what endures, nor can worldly pleasures secure happiness or protect their possessors from God’s wrath. Comfort that leads to divine retribution is neither safety nor fulfilment.

The verse replies circumstantially to their boast: kam is declarative, not interrogative. While they mock the believers by claiming superior conditions, God has destroyed many earlier generations who exceeded them in goods and appearance. Pharaoh held the same conceit, boasting of his kingdom, rivers, and adornment against one he deemed contemptible, and was thereafter drowned with his people and made an example for later generations.
verses.75:
Al-Mizan holds that kāna in man kāna fī al-ḍalāla denotes remaining settled and persistent in error, not merely falling into it. The threatened response is therefore to increase such disbelievers in the material means and worldly allurements that deepen their misguidance. The imperative fa l-yamdud conveys that the Beneficent has made this increase incumbent upon Himself. Although madd and imdād both mean extension, al-Rāghib says that imdād is generally used for desirable things and madd for undesirable ones.

This extension is not a privilege but abandonment disguised as favour: the persistent errant are diverted from truth by worldly glamour until punishment in this life or the Hour comes suddenly. Only then will the truth become manifest, when it can no longer benefit them. Thus they will learn who truly is in the worse plight and has weaker forces, answering their earlier boast about which party had the better abode and assembly.

The singular wording of man governs “his respite,” while its universal meaning governs the plural in “until they see.” At worldly punishment, the disbelievers stand as recipients of chastisement; Al-Mizan identifies the Quraysh elite addressed by these communications with those whose bodies were cast into the wells of Badr. At the Hour they will be in perpetual Hell, and all their numbers and equipment will be futile because none can protect them from God.
verses.76:
Al-Mizan explains al-bāqiyāt al-ṣāliḥat as good deeds preserved in God’s keeping, for which He grants pleasing gratitude and great reward. Thawāb is the recompense that returns to a person for deeds, usually in a good sense, and maradd here means Heaven.

The verse completes the answer to the disbelievers’ claim that their party has the better abode and assembly. Those persisting in error are granted respite, become further absorbed in delusion and worldly distractions, and encounter punishment or the Hour before they can benefit from the truth. In contrast, God increases the rightly guided believers in guidance and grants them success in enduring good works. These yield the best recompense, lead to Paradise, and bring perpetual comfort. The believers’ everlasting bliss is therefore superior to the transient, deceptive attractions possessed by the disbelievers. “With your Lord” indicates that this reward and final outcome rest upon divine reckoning, which does not err.
verses.77:
Al-Mizan takes the verse as an exclamation concerning a class of those who deny God’s communications after hearing the disbelievers’ case against faith. Some who believed in the Prophet, or were considering belief, inclined to the disbelievers and supposed that polytheism, rather than belief in God, would bring worldly wealth, offspring, strength, blessing, and happiness. The fa in “Have you, then, seen” makes this case a logical consequence of the earlier question, “Which of the two parties is best in abiding and best in assembly?” It belongs to the same kind of disbelief: the conviction that all worldly good belongs to the unbelievers and their religion.

The statement “I shall certainly be given wealth and children” concerns this-worldly provision, and its lām of oath and emphatic nūn show that the speaker swears to it. Al-Mizan rejects the majority view, based on a narrated occasion of revelation, that a Quraysh polytheist told Khabbāb b. al-Aratt he would receive wealth and children in Heaven and repay a debt. Since the polytheists did not believe in resurrection, this could only be sarcastic mockery; but a reasoned reply such as “Has he gained knowledge of the unseen, or made a covenant with the Beneficent?” does not answer mere mockery. It also rejects Abū Muslim al-Mufassir’s reported claim that the verse applies to everyone with this characteristic.
verses.78: Al-Mizan explains that the rhetorical question negates the disbeliever’s certainty that disbelief will earn him wealth and children. His claim is conjecture about the unseen: he has neither knowledge of it that would disclose such a reward nor a covenant with the Beneficent that could give him assurance.
verses.79:
Al-Mizan explains kallā as a word of deterrence and rebuke. It rejects the claim that denying God’s communications will bring wealth and children: such provision has other causes, whereas the consequence of this disbelief and conjecture is successive, prolonged chastisement. Thus God records what the speaker says in order to bring about its true consequence, not the prosperity he imagines.

Most likely, “We write down what he says” means that his words and disbelief are made to take root in his heart so that their consequence may take effect. It does not mean merely that the words are entered on his record for Resurrection, as some leading exegetes maintain; on that reading, the following statement, “And We will inherit of him what he says,” would be purposeless repetition.
verses.80:
Al-Mizan interprets God’s inheriting “what he says” to mean that, when the speaker dies, the sin of his assertion—“I will be given wealth and children on account of my disbelief”—remains bound to him as wealth is bound to its owner and passes into God’s custody. This is a metaphor (istiʿāra). He comes to God alone, without the help or support on which he imagined he could rely, carrying the recorded statement for which he will be called to account and undergo prolonged chastisement. This interpretation follows when the wealth and children of verse 77 are understood as worldly.

If, as the majority hold, the statement instead means wealth and children in the Hereafter, verses 78–80 admit another interpretation. The verse then concerns a disbeliever—identified as ʿĀs b. Wāʾil or Walīd b. al-Mughīra—who swore that at resurrection he would receive wealth and children in Heaven. The reply asks whether he has seen the Guarded Tablet, made a covenant with the Beneficent by professing that there is no god but God, or, according to some exegetes, performed good works; it then denies his claim. His words are recorded by the record keepers, his chastisement lengthened, and God inherits the wealth and children to which he refers by causing him to perish and revoking his ownership. He comes to the Hereafter alone, without wealth, children, equipment, or numbers.
verses.81: Al-Mizan explains that the gods taken besides God included Angels, jinns, holy persons, and tyrannical rulers and kings thought to possess celestial sanctity. Their being a “source of strength” meant that they were believed to intercede with God and thereby bring worldly good and avert harm. It cannot mean intercession in the Hereafter, since polytheists do not believe in resurrection.
verses.82:
Al-Mizan explains that a ḍidd is an irreconcilable opposite. Although some dispute al-Akhfash’s view that al-ḍidd may be singular or plural, its singular use for the plural “gods” fittingly conveys that all those deified will unite, like one body, in hostility toward their worshippers.

The pronouns indicate that the supposed gods will reject the polytheists’ worship and become their adversaries, rather than the polytheists rejecting their gods. This accords with the contrast to their formerly being regarded as a source of strength. The reverse interpretation is unlikely both from this reasoning and from the pronoun order; moreover, to say that the polytheists disbelieved in their gods would require “Sa yakfurūn bihim,” whereas kufr bi ʿibādati llah denotes denial of worship, not disbelief in God.

Their rejection on the Day of Resurrection discloses an already existing reality: Resurrection manifests truths rather than bringing them into being. Thus, those deified were already adversaries of their worshippers in this world. On this interpretation, the following “do you not see …” follows consequentially from their rejection of that worship.
verses.83:
Al-Mizan explains azz and hazz as vigorous stirring and disturbance: the Satans incite unbelievers to evil, corruption, and falsehood, shaking them from firmness upon truth. God’s sending them is not pre-emptive misguidance but punishment after the unbelievers’ rejection of truth, as the wording “against the unbelievers” indicates; otherwise it would have said “against them.”

The verse substantiates that the beings deified by the unbelievers are truly their adversaries. The Satans, who are jinn and among their false gods, lead them toward their own doom and wretchedness; they could not do so if they were a source of strength. Yet they act only by God’s permission, hence their activity is called “sending” (ʾirsāl). Al-Mizan rejects the author of Ruḥ al-maʿānī’s attempt to make this verse part of one extended argument beginning earlier in the passage, judging that reading to disrupt both the argument and the links between these verses.
verses.84: Al-Mizan reads ʿadd as both counting and exhausting what is counted: God exhausts a life breath by breath until its appointed term. Yet the verse leaves the object unrestricted, so beyond breaths or days it is really deeds on life’s scroll that are enumerated; these build the person’s eternal condition of comfort or punishment. As a fetus’s body takes shape by remaining in the womb for its term, the soul takes shape during its stay in this world, while God realizes the bounties written for His servant. One should therefore not wish a swift death for either a wicked unbeliever, whose remaining time numbers evil deeds for judgment and punishment, or a good believer, whose time numbers deeds for reward and blessing. The command not to hasten their seizure or judgment follows because they and their gods will ultimately come to God and cannot escape His authority or move without His permission: the apparent delay is His thorough numbering of breaths or deeds.
verses.85: Al-Mizan explains that a wafd is a mounted delegation, with wāfid as its singular. Since being gathered “to the Beneficent” is contrasted with being driven “to Hell,” it apparently means that the God-fearing will be gathered in Heaven, the station of nearness to Him.
verses.86: Al-Mizan explains wird as thirst, apparently derived from wurūd al-māʾ, going to water to drink; it became a metonym for thirst because one goes to drink when thirsty. Calling those driven to Hell “the guilty” states the cause of their fate, just as the preceding verse calls those gathered to the Beneficent God-fearing.
verses.87:
Al-Mizan presents this as a second answer to those who adopt gods in hope of their intercession: not everyone desired or taken as a deity possesses intercession. It is obtainable only through a covenant with God, granted and maintained by a very select number near His presence: And those whom they call upon besides Him have no authority for intercession, but he who bears witness of the truth and they know (him) (43:86).

Some exegetes understand the covenant as belief in God and attestation to Prophethood, so that only its holders may receive intercession; others take it as God’s promise of intercession to Prophets, Imams, believers, and Angels according to oral traditions; still others take it as testifying that there is no god but God, acknowledging one’s powerlessness, and making God one’s sole hope. The commentary judges the first interpretation best suited to the context.
verses.88: Al-Mizan identifies this as the idolaters’ claim. Though some elites may have called certain gods God’s sons honorifically, the masses and some elites taught a literal sonship: a son derived from God’s own nature and sharing his father’s essence. The use of walad, a biological son, rather than ibn, which may also mean an adopted son, shows that this is the claim intended. The following argument through verse 95 refutes it.
verses.89: Al-Mizan explains idd as something evil and abominable, tafaṭṭur as being rent apart, khurūr as falling down, and hadd as destruction. The verses portray the enormity and consequences of ascribing a son to the Beneficent through tangible imagery: the heavens nearly split, the earth nearly cleaves, and the mountains nearly collapse in ruin because of this abominable assertion.
verses.90: Al-Mizan explains idd as something evil and abominable, tafaṭṭur as being rent apart, khurūr as falling down, and hadd as destruction. The verses portray the enormity and consequences of ascribing a son to the Beneficent through tangible imagery: the heavens nearly split, the earth nearly cleaves, and the mountains nearly collapse in ruin because of this abominable assertion.

The verses portray the enormity and consequences of ascribing a son to the Beneficent through tangible imagery: the heavens nearly split, the earth nearly cleaves, and the mountains nearly collapse in ruin because of this abominable assertion.
verses.92:
Al-Mizan explains that everyone’s coming to the Beneficent as a servant describes an abiding reality, not only the Resurrection: all move toward and stand before God under His absolute ownership, unable independently to bring benefit, harm, death, life, or resurrection. His comprehensive knowledge and numbering of them confirm their servitude, like slaves whose provisions, tasks, and functions are fixed after they are entered in a register.

Their coming alone on the Day of Resurrection specifically reveals this reality. All apparent worldly possessions—strength, wealth, children, helpers, and means—will be cut off, and each person will appear empty-handed, owning nothing and shown to have always been wholly a slave.

The verses therefore offer one proof against God’s having a son. Everything in the heavens and earth, including any alleged son, exists only by what God gives, obeys His command without independent choice, is counted and assigned its place and function by Him, and will return to Him alone. Such total need and servitude cannot coexist with a true divine nature derived from His essence. That all things derive their existence from Him is not disputed by those who affirm a Creator; the dispute concerns whether worship and lordship belong to one or to many, including delegated custodians.

Everything in the heavens and earth, including any alleged son, exists only by what God gives, obeys His command without independent choice, is counted and assigned its place and function by Him, and will return to Him alone. Such total need and servitude cannot coexist with a true divine nature derived from His essence. That all things derive their existence from Him is not disputed by those who affirm a Creator; the dispute concerns whether worship and lordship belong to one or to many, including delegated custodians.

verses.96:
Al-Mizan explains wudd and mawadda as love and takes the verse as God’s promise to bring love about for those who believe and do good deeds. Its wording does not restrict that love to believers among themselves or toward others, nor to this world, the Hereafter, or Heaven; such limitations are unwarranted.

Both Shiʿa and Ahl al-Sunna reports give circumstances of revelation, including reports that it was revealed concerning ʿAlī and some Ahl al-Sunna reports concerning those who migrated to Ethiopia. Nevertheless, the general wording is intended, and the verse is likely connected with the statement that the worshippers’ gods will reject their worship and become their adversaries.
verses.97:
Al-Mizan explains that taysīr, making easy, implies that the Qur’an was formerly in a state whose recitation and understanding were inaccessible to people. As God says, “I swear by the Book that makes things clear: Surely We have made it an Arabic Qur’an that you may understand. And surely it is in the original of the Book with Us, truly elevated, full of wisdom (43:2-4).” Had it remained as it is with God, without being made clear (ʿarabī) and recitable, human understanding and intellect could not reach it.

Thus, making the Qur’an easy in the Prophet’s tongue means revealing it in the Arabic, that is, clear, tongue that was his tongue, enabling him to bring good news and warning. Although it may also mean causing it to flow upon his tongue through revelation and granting him divine speech, the first interpretation is better supported by the preceding and related verses and better fits the sūrah’s context. The vehemently contentious people are his people; ludd is the plural of aladd, from ludad, contention.
verses.98: Al-Mizan explains iḥsās as sensory perception and rikz as sound, though rikz is also said to mean ḥiss, sensory perception, or specifically sound. The verse means that however vehemently contentious they are, they cannot overcome God in argument: they should consider the many earlier generations God destroyed, who became extinct, leaving neither a visible trace nor an audible sound.
